**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), P52, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are expected to answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively.

Each essay must contain:
- An introduction = 5 marks

enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION THREE: TEXTUAL STUDY/ ANALYSIS**

**6.** Read the following passage and answer the questions below:

> However, it is a mistake to think that we can remove the degradation of African culture merely by singing and exaggerating the glory and grandeur of this culture- as an end in itself. Those who degraded African culture did not do so because they saw nothing great and glorious in it. They did so simply because it was a culture of the colonized; and degrading it was a way of promoting colonial interest. Therefore in Africa, as long as there are still colonialists and the colonized, or the neo-colonialists and neo-colonized, all talk of African culture will not do anything to revive or promote this culture.
>
> We have to face the iron reality: what is needed as a necessary condition for developing African culture, African philosophy, religion, literature, art and technology- is a change of power relations between Africa and the white world, between the blacks and the whites. Black must not only be beautiful; it must also be powerful. Only then will this beauty matter. To deny this is to forget that while we are busy singing 'black is beautiful' many black girls are busy buying and using white wigs.
>
> *Henry Odera Oruka in Sagacious Reasoning, Edited by Anke Graness and Kai Kresse*

**Questions**

questions.enonce_markdown:
State the main theme and the logical articulations of the text.

(2, 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Main theme and logical articulations of the text (5 marks).**

*Main theme (2 marks).* The passage is about the **conditions for reviving and developing African culture**: praising African culture is not enough, because what is needed first is a change in the power relations between Africa and the white (colonial and neo-colonial) world.

*Logical articulations (3 marks).*
1. *Thesis rejected.* It is a mistake to think that degradation of African culture can be removed by merely singing and exaggerating its glory and grandeur as an end in itself.
2. *Diagnosis.* African culture was degraded not because it lacked greatness but because it was the culture of the colonised, and degrading it served colonial interest.
3. *Consequence.* As long as colonialists and colonised, or neo-colonialists and neo-colonised, remain, speaking about African culture will do nothing to revive or promote it.
4. *Solution.* The necessary condition for developing African culture, philosophy, religion, literature, art and technology is a change in power relations between Africa and the white world, between blacks and whites.
5. *Illustration.* Black must not only be beautiful but also powerful, and to deny this is to forget that while people are busy singing 'black is beautiful', many black girls are busy buying and using white wigs.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain the following phrases as used in the passage:

i. "...the glory and grandeur of this culture"

ii. "degrading it was a way of promoting colonial interest"

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) "...the glory and grandeur of this culture" (2 marks).** The phrase refers to the greatness, splendour and achievements that are attributed to African culture (its history, art, values, kingdoms, traditions). Oruka uses it for the praise by which Africans, in reaction to colonial contempt, celebrate and sometimes exaggerate the value of their heritage. His point is that celebration, taken as an end in itself, is not enough to remove the degradation of African culture.

**(ii) "Degrading it was a way of promoting colonial interest" (2 marks).** The author says that colonisers did not despise African culture because they found it worthless, but because disparaging the culture of the colonised justified domination. If Africans are presented as backward and without culture, then colonial rule, exploitation and the "civilising mission" appear legitimate and beneficial. Contempt for the culture was therefore a *political and economic instrument*, which served the interests of the colonial power, rather than an honest cultural judgement.

questions.enonce_markdown:
According to the author, how can we promote African culture?

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**How to promote African culture, according to the author (4 marks).**

According to Oruka, African culture cannot be promoted by praise and slogans alone. The way is to change the **power relations** between Africa and the white world: the end of colonial and neo-colonial domination and the achievement of real political, economic and technological strength. This is "the necessary condition" for the growth of African philosophy, religion, literature, art and technology.

In practice, this means that Africans must be *powerful* and not only "beautiful": they must control their own resources, institutions, education and technology, so that their culture has respect and influence because it belongs to free and strong societies. Only then will the beauty of black culture "matter". Cultural pride is useful, but it is effective only when it goes with real power and independence.

questions.enonce_markdown:
How is the view in this passage different from the philosophy of Negritude?

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The passage compared with the philosophy of Negritude (4 marks).**

*Negritude* was developed by Aime Cesaire, Leopold Sedar Senghor and Leon-Gontran Damas. It was a reaction to colonial and assimilationist contempt for black people: it affirms the value, identity and contributions of the black world (rhythm, emotion, community, art) and seeks to rehabilitate African culture by celebrating it.

| Point | Negritude | Oruka's view in the passage |
|---|---|---|
| Starting point | Cultural and spiritual affirmation of black identity | Material and political relations of power |
| Means of liberation | Recovering and praising black values and culture | Changing the power relations between Africa and the white world |
| Judgement on celebration | A necessary act of self-assertion and rehabilitation | Insufficient and even misleading if it is an end in itself ("black is beautiful" while many buy white wigs) |
| Emphasis | Identity, culture | Power, politics, economics |

*Similarity:* both want to restore the dignity of Africans and fight the inferiority imposed by colonialism. *Difference:* Negritude emphasises cultural affirmation, while Oruka insists that cultural revival depends on political and economic power. His position is closer to the critics of Negritude (and to Frantz Fanon's idea that culture is bound up with the struggle for liberation) who judged that Negritude was too cultural and too little political.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In what ways has Henry Odera Oruka contributed to the development of African Philosophy?

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Oruka's contribution to the development of African philosophy (4 marks).**

Henry Odera Oruka (Kenyan philosopher, University of Nairobi) is above all known for the following contributions.
- *Sage philosophy.* He led a research project that interviewed wise men and women in traditional communities (the "sages") and recorded their critical and individual reflections. He used it to show that traditional Africa had individual philosophical thought, and not only an unwritten collective worldview.
- *A distinction between folk sagacity and philosophic sagacity.* Folk sagacity is the widely shared wisdom of a community (proverbs, customs); philosophic sagacity is the critical, reasoned thinking of particular individuals who question received beliefs. This was an answer to ethno-philosophy.
- *A classification of trends.* He described the main currents of African philosophy as ethno-philosophy, philosophic sagacity, nationalist-ideological philosophy and professional philosophy, which helped organise the debate.
- *Critical and political engagement.* As in this passage, he linked philosophy with questions of culture, power, justice and human welfare, so that philosophy should respond to the real problems of African societies.

Through these contributions he gave the debate on the existence of African philosophy a new direction and an empirical basis.

questions.enonce_markdown:
What is the relevance of the theme of this passage to the present day African society?

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Relevance of the theme to present-day African society (4 marks).**

The theme (cultural revival depends on real power and not only on praise) remains very relevant.
- *Economic and technological dependence.* Many African countries still depend on foreign markets, loans and technology. Without control of their economies, African languages, arts, education and science struggle to develop, as the author predicts. Initiatives such as continental economic integration and support for local industries and research respond to this need.
- *Cultural alienation.* The "white wigs" example finds echoes today in skin-lightening products, hair and fashion standards, and the dominance of foreign media, music, languages and values. Pride in African culture must go along with real support, for instance teaching national languages, funding local creators, and giving African knowledge a place in schools.
- *Neo-colonial relations.* Questions of unequal trade, foreign influence in politics and control over natural resources show that the author's "iron reality" about power relations still applies.
- *Responsibility of Africans.* It is also a call to Africans themselves to build strong, well-governed institutions, since a culture will be respected only if African societies are able to produce knowledge, wealth and technology.

Hence, the passage asks present-day Africa to join cultural pride with political, economic and technological empowerment.
